records.real_world_identity_notes: Brabham BT26A, the Ford-Cosworth DFV-engined version of the BT26 that finished runner-up in the 1969 World Constructors' Championship. It used a Hewland DG 300 five-speed manual gearbox with a ZF differential.
records.confidence_basis: Simulator behaviour was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the real-world transmission is supported by registered sources.
records.identity_basis: A registered source establishes the BT26A and its gearbox, and the exact simulator identity was observed live.
records.specification_basis: Wikipedia states a Hewland DG 300, 5-speed manual, and the live drive selected five H-pattern gears. Dog-ring engagement is Hewland's design approach rather than a stated property of the DG300, so it is an inference from the make and is recorded as such.
records.confidence_notes: Guided testing directly established five H-pattern gears on a standard gate, the standing-start clutch, the clutchless running shift, and the absence of automatic cut and blip.
control_notes: Simulator behaviour was directly observed in a guided drive in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled. There is no automatic cut or blip, so the driver lifts to upshift.

The standard gate was read from the cockpit by watching the lever and the driver's hand through a shift rather than from a gate plate, which these cars do not have. The same method read three dogleg gates in dataset 0.3.28 that registered sources then corroborated, so it distinguishes the two gates rather than defaulting to one.

The gearbox is a racing Hewland, engaged by dog rings rather than synchronisers, so the driver must match revs on a downshift for the gear to engage cleanly. The downshift blip is therefore required, not optional.

The dog-ring construction of the DG300 is inferred from Hewland's design approach rather than stated by a reviewed source. A source showing the DG300 was synchronised would change the gearbox type and make the downshift blip optional.
